directions.title: Cloth Index — the weave resolves into the garment
directions.plan:
THE IDEA
A garment is cloth that has been cut. So the page shows cloth first, at a scale you can't buy from, and then resolves it into the thing you can buy: an authored technical drawing of that exact garment, on that exact cloth. That single move — weave resolves into drawing, drawing becomes the tile you add to your bag — is the whole visual language, and it repeats nine times without ever becoming decoration, because the drawing IS the product view. Paper #E9E4DA, ink #14120E, a single thread red #9C3A26 for the live/selected state. Bodoni Moda display against IBM Plex Mono spec type and Archivo UI: a couture serif arguing with a factory docket, which is what a Leeds workshop that names its four factories actually is.

PRIMARY JOURNEY (see a-1-page.png, top to bottom)
1. Hero, full viewport: one cloth macro, full bleed, 'Cloth first. Then the garment.' set into the weave. 2. Resolve: the cloth pushes in and dissolves into the Oxford Shirt's technical flat in thread red, with its cloth/cut/colour spec arriving at the margins. 3. The index: the sticky category filter pins under the header (All (9) / Shirts (2) / Outerwear (2) / Trousers (3) / Knitwear (2)) with the live 'Showing N of 9' count; a 3-column grid where every tile is cloth-panel + flat + name + price + colours + fabric + detail sentence + the five-size row with sold-out sizes struck through and unclickable + Add to bag. 4. Bag and Measure side by side: named lines with size and price, Remove per line, running subtotal, the free-delivery bar and remaining-to-£100 amount; the full five-row chest/waist/sleeve chart and the between-sizes advice. 5. Keeping it: four numbered care plates over cloth. 6. Getting it / What people said: all five shipping-and-returns statements, all three reviews with names and what they bought. 7. About: the three shop facts as oversized numerals, then the wordmark.

MOTION — what changes, what drives it, where it resolves (see a-2-transition.png)
Entry: cloth is static and full-bleed; only a slow parallax on the macro. Development: scroll position (not time) scrubs a weave-aligned dissolve — a canvas quantises the cloth into cells whose size follows the fabric's own weave pitch, and the cells retreat to reveal the stroked SVG flat drawing itself in. Exit: the flat does not fade; it is FLIP-transitioned into its tile in the index while the filter bar pins. The same element carries through, so the composition is continuous, reversible, and interruptible — scrubbing back un-draws the shirt. Thereafter, tapping a tile runs the same transition in reverse: the tile's flat expands back to full-frame with its cloth behind it, size row and Add to bag overlaid. One owner per property: a single scroll-progress source drives the canvas cell size and the FLIP; CSS owns hover/press.
Reduced motion: the dissolve becomes a two-step state change (cloth → drawing) with no scrub, the FLIP becomes an instant layout change, parallax is off. The page keeps its structure and every buying control; nothing is only available through the animation.

ASSETS
Sourced (working set already downloaded, provenance in design/_work/manifest.json): nine cloth macros matched to the nine fabric statements — fine shirting for the Oxford, soft weave for the tee, indigo canvas for the Chore Jacket, tweed for the Wool Overshirt, grey herringbone twill for the Pleated Trouser, dark selvedge weave for the Straight Jean, lambswool for the Crew, corduroy/charcoal for the Shawl Cardigan, natural cotton for the Camp Short. All graded to one paper-toned monochrome family so nine different photographers read as one shoot.
Authored: nine SVG technical flats, already drawn and inspected (design/_work/flatsheet.png). Each is drawn to its own detail sentence — three patch pockets and a corozo button front on the Chore Jacket, the single forward pleat on the trouser, the shawl collar on the cardigan, the 7in inseam on the short. These are line drawings and the page says so ('Drawing, not a photograph'), which is exactly how this brief should be honoured: nothing implies verified inventory photography.

MOBILE (see a-3-mobile.png)
Not a squeeze. Hero headline drops to 66px over the same full-bleed cloth; the resolve becomes a single tall frame with the flat centred and the spec below; the index goes one column with a horizontally scrollable filter row; size buttons become full-width 44px+ targets; the bag is a bottom sheet with the same lines, Remove, subtotal and delivery bar. The scroll-scrubbed dissolve stays (it is cheap — one canvas) but runs at a coarser cell size and fewer steps.

IMPLEMENTATION
Vite + React, as the repo already is. Scroll progress from a single IntersectionObserver + rAF-throttled reader; the dissolve on one 2D canvas sized to DPR-capped viewport; the tile transition via measured FLIP (WAAPI) — no smooth-scroll hijack, native scrolling preserved. SVG flats live as components so they can be recoloured and animated without extra requests. Cloth macros emit responsive webp derivatives; originals stay out of the bundle. All content and behaviour come from the existing arrays in src/App.jsx, unchanged.

UNCERTAINTY
The one real risk is the dissolve's legibility at mid-scrub — a cell-quantised cloth can read as mush rather than as a weave becoming a drawing. That is the prototype slice I would build first, at full fidelity with the real Oxford cloth, with its entry and its exit into the index tile, before building anything else. Secondary risk: nine flats must stay visually consistent at tile size on dark cloths (already handled by inverting the stroke on the indigo/denim/corduroy grounds).

COST
Medium. The flats are drawn. The cloth is downloaded. The spend is the dissolve + FLIP and the responsive work.

RECOMMENDED — this one.
Because of the finding in design-blocker.md: no image generator is callable here, and sourced photography cannot honestly represent nine specific fictional garments. Direction A turns that constraint into the concept instead of hiding behind it — cloth is real, the drawing is authored and admits it, and the buy view is the most accurate thing on the page rather than the vaguest. It is also the only one of the two where the memorable motion and the practical task are the same object: what resolves out of the weave is the thing you pick a size from.

directions.title: The Rail — pixel-quantised duotone, horizontal travel
directions.plan: THE IDEA A fashion film, not a catalogue. Near-black #0B0B0A, bone #F3EFE6 and one signal orange #D9531E; every photograph pushed through the same hard duotone so that wildly different source images read as one campaign. Anton at 200px+ against Space Grotesk and mono. The recurring device is block size: images arrive coarsely pixel-quantised and resolve as they reach the centre of attention, so 'coming into focus' is literal and the treatment is the same in the hero, on the rail and in the thumbnails. PRIMARY JOURNEY (see b-1-page.png) 1. Hero: a shop rail at coarse block size behind 'THIRTY STYLES A YEAR.' 2. The rail: a pinned scene where vertical scroll drives garments travelling sideways past camera on three depth layers at different rates, the centred garment fully resolved and its neighbours still in blocks. 3. Buy panel: the resolved garment fills the frame with its number, name, detail sentence, fabric, colours, size row with the sold-out size struck, price and Add to bag. 4. The index, inverted to bone: the sticky filter with all five states and counts, a 3-column grid carrying every garment's full content and size row. 5. Bag + Measure on black. 6. Keeping it (four care facts). 7. Getting it / What people said on bone. 8. The three shop facts and an oversized wordmark. MOTION (see b-2-transition.png) Entry: hero held at coarse block size, slow drift. Development: scroll drives horizontal rail travel; block size is a function of each item's distance from centre, so garments de-pixelate as they arrive and re-pixelate as they leave — the mechanism and the parallax share one scroll value. Exit: the centred garment scales into the buy panel and stays resolved; the block grid persists behind it as texture, so the join reads as arrival rather than a cut. Touch: the rail is also directly draggable with momentum, and drag and scroll write to the same progress value. Reduced motion: no travel and no scrub — the rail becomes a normal horizontally scrollable strip, images render at their resolved block size, section changes are instant. All buying controls unaffected. ASSETS Sourced contextual clothing and workroom photography (rail, hangers, wool coat detail, denim detail, knit, trousers, shorts, folded knitwear), all duotoned to one family. The pixel quantisation is done on canvas at render time, not baked in, so it can be animated. HONEST WEAKNESS This is the reason I am not recommending it. Without a callable image generator, these photographs are representative, not the described garments — and at full-bleed hero scale that shows. The Lambswool Crew stand-in is visibly a puff-sleeved mannequin knit; the Oxford Shirt is a rail of hangers. The page says 'Representative imagery — not a photograph of this garment', which is truthful, but it means the biggest, most cinematic images on the site are also the least informative about what you are buying, and the shopper ends up buying from the text. If you supply real garment imagery, or add an image generator to this session, this direction becomes much stronger and I would revisit it. MOBILE (see b-3-mobile.png) Hero type drops to 78px over the blocked rail; the rail becomes a swipeable snap strip (thumb-driven, same progress value); index is one column on bone with full-width size buttons; bag is a dark sheet with named lines, Remove, subtotal and the free-delivery bar; Measure inverts back to black. IMPLEMENTATION Vite + React. One scroll/drag progress source; the horizontal travel as a transform on a track (native vertical scroll preserved, no smooth-scroll library); pixelation via a small canvas pipeline (draw small, upscale with imageSmoothingEnabled=false) with a resolved swapped in below a block threshold; duotone via blend layers in CSS. Pinned section needs careful interruption handling on iOS. UNCERTAINTY Two. The pinned horizontal scene is the classic place where fast/reverse input and mobile browser chrome break the illusion, and per-frame canvas requantisation of several large images is the only genuinely expensive thing in either direction — it would need a resolution ladder and a frame budget. COST Higher than A: pinned-scroll mechanics, drag parity, a canvas performance ladder, and a light/dark inversion system across the page.
